newsitem.title: UK: Sinn Fein urges UK's Blair to forge new peace.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein urges UK's Blair to forge new peace.

text.p: Gerry Adams, head of the IRA's political arm Sinn Fein, on Sunday urged Britain's incoming Labour government to forge a new peace in the divided province of Northern Ireland.

Adams told a Belfast rally that Prime Minister Tony Blair's landslide election win last week meant he was not dependent on votes of the region's Protestant Unionist legislators that Sinn Fein says kept his predecessor John Major in a stranglehold.
The Unionists want Northern Ireland to remain part of Britain while Sinn Fein represents Catholics who want the province to unite with Ireland.
"What Mr Blair and the British government have to understand is that there is a huge opportunity here for the people of this island to come together in peace and in equality," Adams said.
"He has a majority which unlocks him from the death grip of Unionism...He can bring about a new beginning for the people of his own island and for the people of our island also."
Adams, speaking earlier in an Irish radio interview, said Blair had the power to revitalise paralysed multi-party talks on the future of peace in Northern Ireland.

But, speaking after U.S. President Bill Clinton called for a new Irish Republican Army (IRA) truce to revive peace momentum, Adams signalled that conditions demanded by the guerrillas were not yet in place.

Northern Ireland has been tense in recent months after a series of IRA attacks here and in England which prompted revenge strikes by pro-British Protestant guerrillas. The IRA ended a 17-month ceasefire in February 1996.
Labour says it will not reverse Major's policy that the IRA must call a new truce before Sinn Fein is allowed into talks.
The IRA has repeatedly spurned the demand and Sinn Fein says it should have immediate unconditional entry to all-party talks.
Adams and a senior colleague won landmark victories in last week's election, the first time in some 40 years that Sinn Fein has had two officials voted members of the British parliament.
Although they will not take up their seats, in protest at British rule, their victories were seen by Irish media as strengthening peace hopes.
Adams told Irish radio that Sinn Fein must have a seat in all-party talks to help rebuild the shattered peace process.
"I think what we need to do is first of all to get all of the vexed and contentious issues which have blocked...the search for peace so far," he said.
"In other words, we need a credible, real talks process. The IRA has made its position quite clear that it will enhance...such a peace process."
